topic: quantum query complexity; 1/2-BQP; research-question status tracking
status: resolved-literature-status correction from one sampled full text and one authoritative revised follow-up; not a new unresolved research lead
claim: The 2024 sampled paper's conjecture that 1/2-BQP cannot solve 3-Forrelation is no longer open: the 2025 ECCC paper proves an N^{Ω(1)} query lower bound, and its June 2026 revision says it corrects an important issue in the main-theorem proofs. Any current research-question registry should replace the stale conjecture with the corrected theorem and retain other open hierarchy questions separately.
positive_evidence: The sampled arXiv:2410.08051v1 full text explicitly conjectures that 1/2-BQP cannot solve 3-Forrelation and lists it among open problems.
ECCC TR25-154 revision #1 (accepted 2026-06-18) states a polynomial query lower bound N^{Ω(1)} for 3-Forrelation in 1/2-BQP.
The ECCC revision note explicitly says it corrects an important issue in the earlier main-theorem proofs, making revision-level checking essential.
counterevidence: The later theorem is about query complexity and the specific 3-Forrelation problem, not a complete characterization of 1/2-BQP.
The 2024 paper lists broader open questions about the Forrelation hierarchy and relations to other intermediate quantum models; this one resolved conjecture does not close those questions.
No claim is made here that the result's proof was independently reproduced; the corrected official revision is treated as primary evidence.

sources.sections: ECCC revision abstract and correction note

falsifiable_test: The status claim is overturned if the corrected ECCC revision does not prove an N^{Ω(1)} query lower bound in 1/2-BQP for 3-Forrelation, or if a later correction/erratum withdraws that theorem. Registry utility could be tested by a prospective audit: compare stale-question rates before and after version-aware follow-up searches across a frozen set of candidate open problems. That registry experiment has not been run.
limitations: One sampled quantum-theory paper plus one direct later result; only this precisely worded conjecture is adjudicated. This is not evidence about all open-problem registries or a new theorem discovery.

topic: dynamic algorithms; string, Dyck, and tree edit distance; structured-data maintenance
status: bounded research-design lead from one sampled paper and two purposively selected full-text follow-ups; novelty not established
claim: The audited theory offers asymptotic approximation/update tradeoffs for dynamic string and structured edit distance, while later conditional lower bounds concern exact or combinatorial variants under distinct cost models. The checked papers motivate evolving structured data but do not report a common workload benchmark that measures approximation quality, end-to-end latency, memory, and edit-trace structure together. A demand-matched evaluation could show whether any theoretical regime is useful on real evolving structured documents or code repositories.
positive_evidence: The sampled arXiv:2307.07175v1 theorem parameterizes the approximation factor and amortized expected update time and separately provides a high-probability correctness guarantee.

The full text of arXiv:2510.17799 reports dynamic Dyck/tree approximations, expected amortized updates, and an oblivious-adversary guarantee, and names evolving LaTeX, JSON, XML, and RNA as motivating applications.

The full text of arXiv:2511.09842 states conditional lower bounds for exact weighted or combinatorial unweighted dynamic problems with preprocessing, update, and query costs combined; it explicitly acknowledges the approximate tree-edit algorithm instead of refuting it.
counterevidence: The theoretical papers do establish algorithmic improvements and principled regimes; absence of a benchmark in these audited sources does not imply no practical implementation or evaluation exists elsewhere.
Some application domains may not require exact answers, and worst-case/asymptotic guarantees can be valuable without workload-specific results.

The 2510 follow-up itself includes a deterministic small-distance approximation with polylogarithmic worst-case updates, so one benchmark should not conflate that algorithm with the randomized expected-amortized guarantees.

sources.sections: Theorem 7.10; introduction and fully dynamic update model
Abstract; Introduction Theorems 1.1-1.3 and model definitions
Introduction Questions 1-3; conditional lower-bound theorem statements

falsifiable_test: On versioned JSON/XML/LaTeX and repository edit traces, compare implementations of dynamic string/Dyck/tree approximations with exact recomputation at identical checkpoints and hardware. Stratify by n, true distance, update type, edit burstiness, and adversary assumptions. Record median/tail update and query latency, memory, approximation error, and rebuild frequency. The lead is weakened if no method improves the quality-latency-memory frontier over exact recomputation at realistic sizes; strengthened if gains persist on held-out projects and traces. This benchmark was not run.
limitations: Only three related theoretical sources were deeply checked; two follow-ups were selected purposively, not from the frozen sample. No source search establishing absence of workload evaluations elsewhere was completed, no algorithm was implemented, and no novelty claim is made.

topic: reinforcement learning; computational-statistical gaps; linear function approximation
status: bounded theoretical research-design lead from one sampled full text; novelty not established
claim: The sampled lower bound is strong but precisely scoped: deterministic transitions, two or three actions, H=O(d), linear optimal V* and Q*, specified reward/transition/feature access, and a 1/4-optimal-policy objective. It coexists with polynomial-query statistical learnability and does not itself establish the same computational hardness under stochastic transitions or broader practical RL models. A useful theory program is to alter one assumption at a time and identify which changes preserve hardness versus permit efficient algorithms.
positive_evidence: Theorem 1.1 and the reduction in arXiv:2202.05444v2 establish a conditional polynomial-time lower bound for the formally defined deterministic-transition Linear-2-RL problem.
The paper explicitly distinguishes computational hardness from polynomial-query statistical feasibility, preventing extrapolation to a blanket impossibility claim.
The paper leaves open whether its techniques imply an exponential lower bound under rETH, illustrating that even inside the paper's model the exact computational boundary is not fully settled.
counterevidence: The proof depends on a constructed deterministic MDP and a specific oracle model; stronger structure or altered access assumptions may enable efficient algorithms.
The paper itself notes additional assumptions, such as suboptimality-gap conditions in other work, can matter for computationally efficient learning.
This three-paper cell does not establish that stochastic-transition extensions or other boundary results are absent from the broader RL literature.

sources.sections: Sections 1.1 and 2-3; Theorems 1.1 and 1.5; simulator discussion

falsifiable_test: For each variant, formalize the observation/oracle model and target guarantee; then either prove a reduction from an accepted hard problem or give an algorithm with complexity polynomial in the declared parameters. Change transition determinism, feature access/description, action count, and reward access one at a time. An efficient algorithm in a proposed-hard variant falsifies that hardness claim; an explicit hard instance invalidates a proposed general algorithm. This program was not run and no theorem is claimed.
limitations: One sampled RL theory paper; related literature was not exhaustively searched and no proof was independently reproduced. This is a scoped proof-design direction, not evidence that the proposed boundary is novel or unresolved.
